# Uber Was Cheap. Who Paid?

<!-- TEST FIXTURE for tests/test_checker.py: a real-looking script whose facts
are all in factcheck_clean.md. Written from memory to test the checker; the
facts were NOT checked against their sources. Not the video 1 script. -->

## Cold open

"In 2008, on a snowy night in Paris, Garrett Camp and I had trouble getting a cab."[^F01] That's how Travis Kalanick tells it. Two friends, one cold street, no taxi in sight. What they built next became Uber: you tap your phone, and a car comes to you. But for years, that ride was strangely cheap. Cheaper than it had any right to be. A transport consultant named Hubert Horan went through the numbers Uber showed its own investors, and he came out with an estimate that sounds like a typo. Riders were paying about 41 percent of what each trip really cost.[^F10] So who covered the rest? Not you. Somebody else paid the gap, ride after ride, city after city, for years. This is the story of who paid for your cheap ride.

## The setup

Garrett Camp remembers that night a little differently. He calls it "a pivotal moment," and he is careful to say it was not the beginning: in his telling, the app was already designed before anyone stood in the snow.[^F02] Fine. Founders argue about origin stories all the time. What nobody argues about is the first idea. It was a limo timeshare service: a driver, a luxury car, a parking spot shared by a few friends who wanted to feel rich for an evening.[^F03]

That idea launched in San Francisco in 2010, under a clunky name, UberCab.[^F04] It was a black car on a button. It was not cheap. It was a small luxury for people who already had money, and it made sense as a business. You paid more than a taxi, and you got a nicer car and no waving on the curb.

Then the market changed under its feet. In 2012, a rival called Lyft started putting ordinary people in ordinary cars, with a pink mustache on the front of the car.[^F05] Same year, Uber answered with UberX.[^F06] No limo. No suit. Just a guy with a hatchback and an app. And the price came down, a lot.

Here is the part that matters. Uber was now selling a cheap product, and it was paying for that product with someone else's money. In June 2014, investors put $1.2 billion into the company at a valuation of $17 billion.[^F07] A valuation is just what investors say the whole company is worth, based on what they paid for their slice. Seventeen billion dollars, for a company that lost money on many of its rides. Why would anyone pay that?

## The decision

Because of one bet. Picture Travis Kalanick in those years. He is not a quiet manager. He paces, he talks fast, he treats every city like a battlefield. And he has a simple theory: whoever gets big first wins, and the winner can fix the prices later.

So Uber made a choice, and it made it again and again. It would charge riders less than a ride cost. It would pay drivers bonuses on top of their fares, to keep them on the road. And it would cover the difference with investor money, for as long as investors kept writing checks. There's a word for that gap: a subsidy, which means someone other than the buyer covers part of the price. You weren't buying a ride. You were buying a ride with a discount that a stranger had paid for.

It worked, at least on the street. Riders loved it. Why would you call a taxi, wait twenty minutes and pay cash, when a car could reach you in a few minutes for less? Taxi companies could not match those prices, because they had to make a profit on every trip. Uber didn't. Not yet.

Now picture the other side of the windshield. A driver logs in at six in the morning, because the app promised a bonus if he finishes enough trips before the weekend. He doesn't own a limo. He owns a used sedan, and he is still paying for it. Every ride he accepts is cheap for you and a little cheaper for him than it looks, because the gas, the tires and the miles are all his. He keeps driving anyway. The bonus is real, the payout lands every week, and for a while the math seems to work. What he cannot see from the driver's seat is where that bonus comes from. It isn't coming from you. It's coming from a fund on the other side of the world, through an app that loses money on his trip.

But a subsidy has to come from somewhere. Every cheap ride was a small hole in the company's pocket, and there were millions of rides. In 2016, Uber lost about $2.8 billion, not counting its business in China.[^F11] That same summer, it gave up on China and sold its operations there to Didi, the local rival it could not outspend.[^F09]

## Follow the dollar

So let's follow your dollar, one step at a time. When you paid for a ride in those years, where did the money go, and who made up the difference?

Step one: the investors. They paid first, and they paid the most. In 2016, Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund alone put $3.5 billion into Uber.[^F08] Think of it as a prepaid card for the whole city. Every time you got a discount, a little of that card was used up. The investors were not being generous, of course. They were betting that one day Uber would own the market, and that its shares would be worth far more than they paid. Until that day, their cash bought your cheap rides.

Step two: the drivers. Uber kept a cut of every fare, often 20 to 25 percent.[^F12] The rest went to the driver. But the driver paid for the car, the fuel, the insurance and the repairs. Those costs don't show up on your receipt. They show up in the driver's bank account, months later, when the transmission goes.

Think about what that means for a single trip. You see a fare. The driver sees the same fare, minus Uber's cut, minus the gas he burned getting to you, minus the slow wear on a car he will have to replace sooner than he planned. None of that appears on any screen. The company counts him as a partner, not an employee, so the car is his problem, and so is the bill when it breaks. And the promises were sometimes bigger than the paychecks. In January 2017, Uber agreed to pay $20 million to settle charges from the Federal Trade Commission that it had exaggerated how much drivers could earn.[^F13] So part of your cheap ride was paid by people who thought they would make more than they did.

Step three: the people who were already there. Before Uber, a taxi in New York needed a medallion, a permit sold by the city. In 2013, a medallion could sell for more than $1 million.[^F14] Drivers took out loans to buy them. Families treated them like a house: something you pay off, and then it pays you. When cheap rides flooded the streets, the value of those medallions collapsed. Nobody sent those drivers a check. Their savings paid for the price war too.

It's worth stopping on that for a second, because it is the least visible payer in the whole story. A medallion owner did not lose money on any single ride. Nobody took cash out of his wallet. What he lost was the thing he had been counting on to retire: the right to sell his permit to the next driver for a good price. That kind of loss never shows up as a line on a bill. It shows up years later, as a loan that can't be paid and a plan that quietly falls apart.

That is the machine. Investors paid with cash. Drivers paid with their cars and their time. Taxi owners paid with their savings. And you, the rider, paid the least of anyone. For a while.

## What it cost

The bill started to arrive in 2017. In June of that year, after months of scandals inside the company, Travis Kalanick resigned as chief executive.[^F15] In August, the board picked Dara Khosrowshahi, who had run the travel site Expedia, to replace him.[^F16] His job was not to win the war. His job was to make the war pay.

Then came the stock market. In May 2019, Uber sold shares to the public for the first time, an IPO, which means anyone with a brokerage account could now own a slice. The price was $45 a share, and the sale raised $8.1 billion.[^F17] The filing that came with it was unusually blunt. Right near the top of its list of risks, Uber wrote: "We have incurred significant losses since inception."[^F18] That year, it lost $8.5 billion.[^F19]

Wall Street noticed. On the first day of trading, the shares closed below the price the bankers had set, which is not how a celebration is supposed to go. For the first time, the people paying for the subsidy were not a handful of large funds in private meetings. They were ordinary savers, through their retirement accounts and index funds, who now owned a piece of a company that had never made a profit. The bet had been handed to the public.

And the drivers? Their fight moved to the voters. In California, a law would have made many of them employees, with a minimum wage and benefits. Uber, Lyft and DoorDash answered with a ballot measure, Proposition 22, and spent more than $200 million to pass it.[^F20] In November 2020, voters said yes, and the drivers stayed contractors. Across the ocean, it went the other way. In February 2021, the Supreme Court of the United Kingdom ruled that Uber drivers were workers, with a right to holiday pay and a minimum wage.[^F21]

Still, the losses kept coming. In 2022, Uber lost $9.1 billion, a figure inflated by the falling value of the stakes it held in other companies.[^F22] Then, in 2023, something happened that had never happened before. Uber made $1.1 billion of operating profit over a full year.[^F23] Operating profit is the money a company makes from its own business, before gains or losses on its investments. In other words, the rides finally paid for themselves.

How? Partly by getting more efficient. Partly by charging more. If you take Uber today, you may have noticed that it is not the bargain it used to be. The prices crept up, the bonuses for drivers shrank, and the discounts that used to show up every week became rare. The subsidy did not vanish. It was simply handed back to the people who had been enjoying it: the riders.

## The lesson

So who paid for your cheap ride? First the investors, who spent billions on a bet. Then the drivers, who carried costs that never appeared on your receipt. Then the taxi owners, whose savings evaporated. And finally you, a little more every year, once the war was won and the discounts were gone.

None of this was a secret, exactly. The losses were in the filings. The driver lawsuits were in the news. The medallion loans were in the courts. But a cheap ride is a very good way to stop people from asking questions. When something costs you almost nothing, you don't wonder who is covering it. You just tap the button again. That is not a flaw in you. It is how the strategy was designed to work, and it worked on almost everyone, including the people who wrote about it.

That's the pattern to remember. When a product is cheaper than it should be, it is not a gift. Somebody is paying for it, and usually somebody who never agreed to. Next time an app hands you a price that seems too good, ask yourself one question: whose dime is this?

In the next video, we follow the cleaning fee on your Airbnb bill, because that one has a payer you would never guess.[^F24] And tell us in the comments: what "free" thing should we follow next?
